theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Person of Christ, Incarnation
summary: The eternal Son became flesh; one person, two natures; truly God and truly man
readingInstruction: Read John 1:1-18, Philippians 2:5-11, and Colossians 1:15-20. Today is a doctrinal pause on the person of Christ: who he is, and what it means that the Word became flesh. Notice what each passage says about his divinity and his humanity.
settingTheScene: Three of the greatest passages about Christ in the New Testament come from two authors. John writes a prologue to his Gospel. Paul, writing from prison to the Philippians, quotes what is probably an early hymn. In Colossians, he answers a church troubled by false teaching and puts Christ above all. The church has summarized these teachings in the doctrine of the incarnation: that the eternal Son took on a true human nature without ceasing to be God.
observation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
“Who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6).
“But emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7).
“And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8).
“And every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).
“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15).
“For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell” (Colossians 1:19).
doctrinalFocus: The incarnation is the central miracle of the Christian faith: the eternal Son of God, the second person of the Trinity, took to himself a true human nature, with a body and a soul, and was born of the virgin Mary. He did not stop being God; he added humanity. The church confessed at Chalcedon in AD 451 that Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man, “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” Christians have long held this because the Scriptures teach both halves. Jesus is called God, worshiped, and credited with creating all things. And he hungers, thirsts, weeps, grows weary, suffers, and dies. If he were not truly God, he could not save us. If he were not truly man, he could not stand in our place. “Emptied himself” in Philippians 2 does not mean he gave up his divine nature, but that he laid aside the privileges of glory and took the form of a servant. The incarnation is the beginning of his work of redemption: the one who became what we are, so that we might become what he is, children of God.
interpretation:
John tells us who the Word is. He was with God and was God, the agent of creation, the source of life and light. Then comes the most astonishing sentence of the Bible: “The Word became flesh.” The one who made the world entered it. Notice that John does not say the Word “appeared” to be flesh or “entered” a body. He became flesh. He took our nature and lived among us.

Paul gives the path of the incarnation in Philippians 2. Christ Jesus was in the form of God, and did not treat equality with God as something to hold on to. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He humbled himself, became obedient, and went all the way to death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.” The pattern is descent and ascent. Paul’s reason for telling the story is practical: “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.” The incarnation is also a model for humility.

In Colossians, Paul speaks of the cosmic Christ. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, which means supreme in rank and not first created, for “by him all things were created.” He holds all things together. He is the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead. All the fullness of God dwells in him, and through him God reconciles all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross.

Put these three together. The one who made the stars became a baby. The one who holds the universe together was carried by his mother. The one who is Lord of all died on a cross. This is why the church has always been amazed. Our salvation depends on who he is.
connection: Isaiah 9:6 calls the child “Mighty God.” Isaiah 45:23 is the verse Paul uses in Philippians 2:10-11. Hebrews 1:1-4 and 2:14-18 speak of the Son’s deity and humanity. 1 Timothy 3:16 calls it a great mystery. 1 John 4:2 says every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. Galatians 4:4 says God sent his Son, born of woman. Luke 1:35 says the child will be called holy, the Son of God.
application:
Say the Chalcedonian summary aloud: Jesus is fully God and fully man, one person. Thank him for each half.

Read Philippians 2:5 again. Where is Christ calling you to take the form of a servant?

When you feel that God is far away, remember that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
prayerPrompts: Worship Jesus, the Word who was with God and was God.
Thank him for emptying himself and taking the form of a servant.
Tell him what it means that he became one of us.
